title: Lobbyists who are also something else to the official
question: Which lobbying firms are also paid by the campaigns of officials they lobby, which lobbyists used to be the officials, and which officials report income from a lobbying firm?
finding: Campaign committees of 8 officials and candidates paid $649,254 since 2010 to firms that sell lobbying (8 official-and-firm pairs of $1,000 or more). In 5 pairs ($397,453) the same firm’s lobbyists reported contacting that official, and in 5 a payment and a contact fall within two years of each other. 13 registered lobbyists carry the name of someone lobbyists had earlier reported contacting ten or more times as an official and then lobbied that same office; 0 did so within a year of their last recorded contact as an official. 9 City officials or employees report income from a firm that sells lobbying.
how: Four records. (1) Payments made by officials’ campaign committees (Form 460 Schedule E) whose payee name equals a firm that sells lobbying, set beside that firm’s reported contacts with the same official. Payments coded as returned contributions are left out; code meanings are read from the legend on a Form 460 in the document library. (2) Names that appear first as a contacted official at least ten times and later as a registered lobbyist who contacts the same office, kept only when the surname and first name together are rare among everyone named in the lobbying file and on Form 700 cover pages; the gap runs from the last contact received to the first contact made with the former office. (3) Income sources on officials’ Form 700 that equal a lobbying firm’s name. (4) The Ethics Commission’s table of campaign consultants who employ City officeholders. Former City employees who became lobbyists, found from the payroll, are in the site’s “People and roles” page (screen revolving-door), which also explains the one-year rule.
limits: Many firms both run campaigns and lobby; Campaign consultants file their own reports with the Ethics Commission. The firm-name match can catch a different business with the same name, and the former-official rows are name matches: two people can share a name, and the last date a lobbyist reported contacting someone is not the date that person left office. Income from a lobbying firm is often a spouse’s salary, pay from a job held before joining the City, or work that has nothing to do with the official’s department. No record shows which official a former aide worked for, so staff cannot be tied to a particular supervisor. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made.
